<reason>CON (A) built the more decisive path. Its opening set up a coherent "proxy fails" case (exposure vs. silhouette, insurance risk-rating, cliff effects), and its pressure questions landed real burdens: the unnamed fee level and the threshold's actual scope. A answered B's pressure questions directly with clean A1/A2 labels, distinguishing cost-recovery tools that track use from a static surcharge sold as safety. A's closing crystallized sharply: even granting B's "size is the cost" theory, the motion as written charges a category tier, not per-foot or per-pound, and never touches velocity or miles. B's case had genuine strengths—the externality logic, "physical proxies are how all pricing works," and the good closing reframe that curb space is measured in feet—but B's Rebuttal 2 visibly shifted ground ("cost recovery alone justifies it; behavior change is the bonus"), which A exploited as abandoning the safety rationale. B also claimed CON "never answered" the pure-tax question before CON's answering speech arrived, and B's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for length, an execution cost that cut off its final comparison. B's fallback to subsidy-elimination is legitimate but came late and underdeveloped relative to A's sustained instrument-mismatch attack.</best_rebuttal>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1-A4.3): it cleanly split B's pure-tax dilemma by distinguishing use-scaled cost recovery from a static size surcharge sold as pedestrian safety, then flagged B's shift to "cost recovery alone justifies it"—the pivotal moment where PRO's opening safety story quietly became a revenue argument, a concession A hammered through the closing.</best_rebuttal>
